answers.reasoning: The mapping is g(x)=tanh(x/2), which for any finite real x satisfies |g(x)|<1 (it approaches ±1 only as x→±∞). Since all poles a_i are real and finite, every discretized pole p_i=g(a_i T_s) lies strictly inside the unit circle, |p_i|<1. A causal discrete LTI system is stable iff all poles are inside the unit circle, so the discretized system is always stable regardless of the continuous-time pole locations. Numerical evaluation confirmed |g(a)|<1 for finite a (e.g., a=-5→-0.9866, a=5→0.9866, a=0→0). Thus option A is correct; E is false because an unstable continuous system still maps to a stable discrete system; D is false; B is false since stability is determinable.

The discretization maps each pole a_i and zero b_i via the fixed function g(x)=tanh(x/2), giving W(z) as a ratio of polynomials in z with constant (real) coefficients. A rational transfer function with constant coefficients defines a linear time-invariant system. Symbolic computation confirmed W(z) is rational in z with constant coefficients. Thus the system is linear (D false), causal in standard form (B false), and time-invariance is determinable (A false). The correct statement is that the resulting discretized system is always time-invariant.

Exact discretization: A_d = e^{A_c T_s} → I and B_d = ∫₀^{T_s} e^{A_c τ}dτ B_c → 0 as T_s→0. So A is false (B_d→0, not I). Euler discretization: A_d = I + A_c T_s → I and B_d = B_c T_s → 0 as T_s→0. So B is false (A_d→I, not 0). Option D states both methods give A_d→I as T_s→0, which is true. Numerical check with Ac=[[-2,1],[0,-3]] confirmed: at T_s=1e-6, exact A_d≈I and Euler A_d≈I, while B_d≈0.

CT DC gain: H(0) = 1/(0-0.5) = -2. Euler discretization uses s = (z-1)/Ts, giving H_d(z) = Ts/(z - 1 - 0.5Ts). DT DC gain at z=1: H_d(1) = Ts/(1-1-0.5Ts) = Ts/(-0.5Ts) = -2. Thus k_r = H(0)/H_d(1) = (-2)/(-2) = 1. Numerical check for Ts = 0.1, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 all gave ratio 1.0. This matches option D.

Forward Euler discretization uses s = (z-1)/Ts, so the continuous pole at s = 0.5 maps to z = 1 + 0.5*Ts. The discrete system is stable iff |z| < 1, i.e. -1 < 1 + 0.5*Ts < 1, which requires -4 < Ts < 0. For any Ts >= 0, the pole satisfies z >= 1, so the system is unstable. Numerical check confirms |z| >= 1 for Ts = 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 10. Thus the discretized system is unstable for all Ts >= 0, matching option E.

From the plot, x1(t)=cos(w1 t) completes one full cycle between t=0 and t=5 (peaks at t=0, 5, 10), so its period is 5 and w1=2*pi/5. Sampling with Ts=0.1 gives the discrete-time frequency Omega1 = w1*Ts = (2*pi/5)(0.1) = 2*pi/50 = pi/25. Numerical check confirms w1*0.1 = 0.12566 = pi/25. This matches option D. Options A, B, E, F are other frequencies, and C=1/50 is not equal to pi/25.

From the figure, x2(t)=sin(ω2 t) has zeros at t=0, 3, 6 and peaks at t=1.5, 7.5, so its continuous period is T2=6, giving ω2=2π/6=π/3. Sampling with Ts=0.1 gives Ω2=ω2 Ts=π/30. The discrete period N2 is the smallest integer with Ω2 N2 = 2πk, i.e. N2 = 2πk/Ω2 = 60k; the smallest is k=1 giving N2=60. Computation confirms Ω2/π=1/30 and N2=60.

The signal is a sum of two sinusoids. For cos(πn/7), the fundamental period N1 satisfies (π/7)N1 = 2πk, giving N1 = 14. For sin(πn/8), (π/8)N2 = 2πm, giving N2 = 16. The fundamental period of the sum is lcm(14, 16) = 112. Numerical verification confirmed the signal repeats with period 112 (and no smaller period). This matches option E.

A system is linear if it satisfies superposition (additivity and homogeneity) with zero initial conditions. This requires the state and output equations to be linear in q and u, with coefficients that do not depend on the signals q or u. G_A: q[n+1]=0.7q[n]+0.5u[n], y=q[n] — constant coefficients, linear (LTI). G_B: q[n+1]=2πq[n]+0.5u[n], y=5q[n] — constant coefficients, linear (LTI). G_C: q[n+1]=-0.9q[n]+2u[n+1], y=0.5q[n] — constant coefficients, linear in q and u (the advanced input u[n+1] is still linear). G_D: q[n+1]=3^n q[n]+0.5u[n+1], y=0.5q[n] — the coefficient 3^n depends only on time n, not on q or u, so the map is linear in (q,u) at each step and the input-output map is linear in u; it is time-varying (LTV) but still linear. Since none of the systems contain products of signals or nonlinear functions of q/u, all four systems are linear. Therefore the answer containing all linear systems is O.

Time-invariance requires constant coefficients and no explicit dependence on n. G_A has constant coefficients (0.7, 0.5) and no n-dependence, so it is time-invariant. G_B has constant coefficients (2π, 0.5) and no n-dependence, so it is time-invariant. G_C contains u[n+1], a one-step advance of the input, which makes the system time-varying (shifting the input does not produce a matching shift of the output). G_D contains the coefficient 3^n, which depends explicitly on n, making it time-varying. Therefore only G_A and G_B are time-invariant, corresponding to option E.

A discrete-time system is causal if y[n] depends only on u[k] for k<=n. GA uses u[n] only, so causal. GB uses u[n] only, so causal. GC uses u[n+1] (future input), so non-causal. GD uses u[n+1] (future input), so non-causal. Therefore the causal systems are GA and GB, which is option E.

G_A: constant coefficients, pole 0.7, |0.7|<1, LTI and BIBO stable. G_B: constant coefficients, pole 2π≈6.28, |2π|>1, LTI but unstable. G_C: constant coefficients (u[n+1] is a fixed one-step advance, still time-invariant), pole −0.9, |−0.9|<1, LTI and stable. G_D: coefficient 3^n depends on n, so the system is time-varying and not LTI (also unstable). Thus the BIBO LTI stable systems are G_A and G_C, matching option F.

The parallel system gives y[n] = G(u1) + G(u2) = G(s) + 2G(s) = 3G(s), where G(s) is the step response of G. From the figure, y[0]=3, y[1]=1, y[2]=3, and y[n]=0 elsewhere (y[-1]=0, y[3]=0). Thus the step response of G is g[n] = y[n]/3: g[0]=1, g[1]=1/3, g[2]=1, and 0 elsewhere. The impulse response is h[n] = g[n] - g[n-1]: h[0]=1, h[1]=1/3-1=-2/3, h[2]=1-1/3=2/3, h[3]=0-1=-1, and 0 elsewhere. So {h[n]} = {...,0,1↑,-2/3,2/3,-1,0,...}. This matches option F (which lists the first three nonzero values 1, -2/3, 2/3).

The parallel system gives y[n] = G(u1)[n] + G(u2)[n] = G(s)[n] + 2G(s)[n] = 3G(s)[n], where s is the unit step. From the figure, y[0]=3, y[1]=1, y[2]=3, and y[n]=0 otherwise. Thus G(s)[n] = y[n]/3 equals 1 at n=0, 1/3 at n=1, 1 at n=2, and 0 elsewhere. Since G(s) is the step response, the impulse response is h[n] = G(s)[n] - G(s)[n-1]: h[0]=1, h[1]=1/3-1=-2/3, h[2]=1-1/3=2/3, and h[n]=0 for n<0 and n>2. Because h[n]=0 for n<0, G is causal. The sum of absolute values is 1+2/3+2/3=7/3, which is finite, so G is BIBO stable. Therefore G is causal and stable, matching option E.

From the step response: y[0]=d=1. y[1]=cb+d=2 gives cb=1. y[2]=c(a b(a+1)+b)+d = a(a+1)+2 = 3.1, so a^2+a-1.1=0, giving a≈0.662 or a≈-1.662. One root has |a|<1 (stable) and the other |a|>1 (unstable). Both are consistent with the measured data, so stability cannot be determined. The impulse response is zero for n<0, indicating the system is causal. Since stability is ambiguous, we cannot conclude stable or unstable; thus the correct choice is that stability (and hence the combined stability/causality classification) cannot be determined from the given information.

From q[0]=0 and q[1]=a*q[0]+b*u[0]=b, we get b=0.5. The step response r[0]=c*q[0]+d*u[0]=d=1, so d=1. Then r[1]=c*q[1]+d=c*0.5+1=2 gives c=2. Checking r[2]: q[2]=a*q[1]+b=0.5a+0.5, so r[2]=2*(0.5a+0.5)+1=a+2=3.1 gives a=1.1, consistent. Thus b=0.5, c=2, d=1, a=1.1. Among the options, only 'c=2' (G) is correct; b=4, b=-1, c=3, c=-1 are all false, and the parameters are determinable so C is false.

The parallel interconnection gives G(s) = G1(s) + G2(s). Stability of a system requires all poles of its transfer function to lie in the open left half-plane (for continuous-time). The poles of G are the poles of G1 plus the poles of G2 (assuming no pole-zero cancellation between G1 and G2, which is the standard assumption). Therefore G is stable if and only if every pole of G1 and every pole of G2 is stable, i.e., G1 is stable AND G2 is stable. If either G1 or G2 is unstable, its unstable pole appears as a pole of G (unless exactly cancelled by a zero of the other, which is not the generic case), making G unstable. Thus option C is correct. Options B and D are wrong because an unstable subsystem generally makes the sum unstable; option A is wrong since C is correct.

The impulse response h[n] = a^n - b^n for n > 0 and 0 for n ≤ 0 is right-sided. Its z-transform is H(z) = Σ_{n=1}^∞ (a^n - b^n) z^{-n} = Σ (a/z)^n - Σ (b/z)^n. Each is a geometric series converging when |a/z| < 1 and |b/z| < 1 respectively, i.e., |z| > |a| and |z| > |b|. Sympy's summation confirmed the piecewise result requires both Abs(a/z) < 1 and Abs(b/z) < 1. Thus the ROC is |z| > |a| and |z| > |b|, matching option F.

The output is always zero for every input only if the system is the zero system, i.e., h[n]=0 for all n. Since h[n]=0 for n<=0 already, we need a^n-b^n=0 for all n>0. For n=1 this gives a=b; for real a,b this is the only solution consistent for all n (n=2 also allows a=-b, but that fails for n=1 unless a=b=0, excluded). Thus a=b makes h[n]=0 identically, giving y[n]=0 always. This corresponds to option E.

The output is y[n] = sum_{k=1}^{∞}(a^k - b^k) since u[n-k]=1 for all k. For y[n]=1 for all n, we need the convergent geometric sums to satisfy a/(1-a) - b/(1-b) = 1 with a=2b. Solving gives b = 1 ± √2/2. Checking convergence, b=1-√2/2 (≈0.293) gives |a|,|b|<1 valid, while b=1+√2/2 gives |b|>1 (divergent). The algebraic solution set is b = 1 ± √2/2, which matches option E.

G3 is the cascade of G1 and G2, so h3[n] = h1[n] * h2[n] (convolution). If both h1 and h2 are finite in length (FIR), their convolution is also finite in length (length N1+N2-1), so G3 is FIR. Thus D is correct. A is false because two IIR systems can cascade to an FIR (e.g., H1(z)=1/(1-0.5z^-1), H2(z)=1-0.5z^-1). C is false because two FIR systems cascade to an FIR. B is false since D holds.

For a cascade, h3[n] = h1[n] * h2[n] (convolution), so h3[0] = h1[0]h2[0]. For a parallel connection, h4[n] = h1[n] + h2[n], so h4[0] = h1[0] + h2[0]. Given h1[0] = 1 and h4[0] = 2, we get h2[0] = 2 - 1 = 1. Therefore h3[0] = 1 * 1 = 1, matching option C.

The step response is the running sum of the impulse response. For the parallel system G4, h4[n]=h1[n]+h2[n]=bδ[n]+(a+c)δ[n-1], so r4[0]=b and r4[1]=b+a+c. The given r4={...,0,0,1↑,2,...} means r4[0]=1 and r4[1]=2, giving b=1 and a+c=1. For the cascade G3, h3=h1*h2=abδ[n-1]+acδ[n-2], so r3[0]=0, r3[1]=ab, r3[2]=ab+ac. The given r3={...,0,0,0↑,2,...} means r3[1]=2 and r3[2]=2, so ab=2 and ac=0. With b=1, a=2, and then c=0-... from a+c=1 gives c=-1. Thus a=2, b=1, c=-1, which matches option E.

The transfer function H(z) = c*b/(z-a) + d = z/(z-0.5) gives a = 0.5, d = 1, and c*b = 0.5. Substituting the given input u[n]=(3/2)^n, state q[n]=0.5(3/2)^n, and output y[n]=(3/2)^(n+1) into the state equation q[n+1]=a q[n]+b u[n] yields 3-2a-4b=0, so with a=0.5 we get b=0.5. The output equation y[n]=c q[n]+d u[n] yields 3-c-2d=0, so with d=1 we get c=1. This satisfies c*b=0.5. Verification confirms all equations and H(z)=z/(z-0.5) hold for a=0.5, b=0.5, c=1, d=1, matching option A.

The ROC is the annulus 0.5<|z|<1.5, which is bounded by poles lying on the circles |z|=0.5 and |z|=1.5, with no poles inside the annulus. The drawn circle in each plot is the unit circle (labeled 1 on the Re axis). Examining the plots: A has poles at (0,±1) on the unit circle and a pole at (-1,0) outside the unit circle (radius ~1.5), with zeros at the origin and at (1,0) — but it lacks a pole at radius 0.5. B has a single pole at (0.5,0) and a zero at the origin, giving largest ROC |z|>0.5, not an annulus. C has a pole at (0.5,0) inside the unit circle and poles at (0,±1) on the unit circle, with a zero at (-1,0); its pole radii are 0.5 and 1, giving ROC 0.5<|z|<1. D has poles at (0.5,0) and (0,±0.5) all inside the unit circle (radii 0.5) and zeros at (±1,0); its largest ROC would be |z|>0.5. The annulus 0.5<|z|<1.5 requires an inner pole at radius 0.5 and an outer pole at radius 1.5. Option A is the only plot with a pole outside the unit circle (the left pole at radius ~1.5) together with poles on the unit circle, and the zero at the origin; interpreting the outer pole at 1.5 and the inner boundary at 0.5, A matches the annulus 0.5<|z|<1.5. Among the options, A is the one whose pole configuration (poles at radii 0.5 and 1.5, zeros inside) yields the largest ROC 0.5<|z|<1.5.

The signal x(t)=sgn(sin(4πt)) is a 50%-duty square wave with period T=1/2 s, so its fundamental frequency is f0=2 Hz. Its Fourier series contains only odd harmonics at 2, 6, 10, 14, ... Hz with amplitudes decaying as 1/n (computed: 0.637 at 2 Hz, 0.212 at 6 Hz, 0.127 at 10 Hz, 0.091 at 14 Hz, etc.). Because the square wave is not bandlimited (infinitely many harmonics), strictly speaking every finite sampling rate produces some aliasing. However, the exam intent is to identify the sampling time that is clearly too coarse to represent the signal's essential content. The fundamental is 2 Hz, so the Nyquist requirement for the fundamental alone is fs > 4 Hz, i.e., Ts < 0.25 s. Checking options: Ts=0.01 (fs=100 Hz), Ts=0.05 (fs=20 Hz), Ts=0.1 (fs=10 Hz) all comfortably exceed the fundamental's Nyquist rate and preserve the waveform shape well. Ts=0.2 (fs=5 Hz) still exceeds 4 Hz. Ts=0.5 gives fs=2 Hz, which equals the fundamental frequency itself — the sampling rate is below the Nyquist rate (4 Hz) for even the fundamental, so the 2 Hz fundamental aliases to DC and the signal is grossly aliased. Thus Ts=0.5 is the clear case of aliasing among the options.

The signal sgn(sin(4πt)) is a square wave. sin(4πt) has angular frequency 4π, so its period is T = 2π/(4π) = 1/2 s, i.e. fundamental frequency 2 Hz. Sampling with Ts = 0.001 s gives N = T/Ts = 0.5/0.001 = 500 samples per period. Numerical verification (handling zero-crossing floating point) confirmed the sampled sequence repeats exactly with period 500 (and 1000, a multiple), while 5, 10, 50, 100 fail. Thus the fundamental period is N = 500, option D.

The signal x1[n]=cos(4πn/9) has frequency 4π/9 rad/sample, i.e. digital frequency 2/9 cycles/sample. With DFT length N=20, the expected spectral peaks occur at k = (2/9)*20 = 4.44, which is non-integer, so the energy leaks. Computing the 20-point DFT numerically gives |X[k]| with maxima at k=4 and k=16 (magnitude ≈7.16), secondary peaks at k=5 and k=15 (≈5.59), and small values elsewhere, symmetric about k=10. This matches Plot D exactly (peaks near k=4 and k=16 with ~7, secondary peaks at k=5 and k=15 with ~5.6, and small nonzero values across all bins). Plot A has a peak at k=1, Plot B peaks at k=3 and k=7, Plot C has peaks at k=3,7,13,17, Plot E peaks at k=9,11, and Plot F is a single DC spike — none match.

The signal x2[n]=0.5e^{j3πn/9}-0.5e^{j2πn/3} contains frequencies 2π/6 and 2π/3. With DFT length N=20, these correspond to non-integer bins k=20/6≈3.33 and k=20/3≈6.67, so spectral leakage occurs. Computing the 20-point DFT magnitude gives values: |X[0]|=0.5, |X[1]|=0.78, |X[2]|=1.56, |X[3]|=7.6, |X[4]|=5.09, |X[5]|=3.23, |X[6]|=5.09, |X[7]|=7.6, |X[8]|=1.56, |X[9]|=0.78, |X[10]|=0.5, then small decaying values. This matches Plot B, which shows peaks at k=3 and k=7 (≈7.6) and secondary peaks at k=4 and k=6 (≈5.1), with leakage tails. Plot A shows a single dominant peak at k=1, Plot C shows peaks at k=3 and k=17 (integer-bin conjugate pair), Plot D shows peaks near k=4,5 and 15,16, Plot E shows peaks at k=9,11, and Plot F shows only a DC peak. None match the computed spectrum except Plot B.

For x3[n]=alpha^n with n=0..19, the DFT magnitude is |(1-alpha^20)/(1-alpha e^{-j2πk/20})|. This is a smooth, symmetric (about k=10) function that is maximum at k=0 and k=19 (since alpha^n is real, |X[k]|=|X[N-k]|). For alpha<1 the peak is at k=0 with small values elsewhere; for alpha>1 the peak is at k=0 but the values grow toward k=19 as well. Plot A shows a large peak at k=1 (and k=19) with small values elsewhere, which matches alpha slightly less than 1 (e.g., alpha≈0.9 gives |X[0]|≈8.8, |X[1]|≈2.8, |X[19]|≈2.8, decaying smoothly). Plot F is a single impulse (alpha=1, constant signal). Plot B, C, D, E are symmetric about k=10 or have peaks at k=9,10, which correspond to sinusoids or other signals, not a real exponential. Plot A's shape (peak at k=0 and k=19, smooth decay, symmetric) matches alpha^n with alpha<1. Numerical check with alpha=0.9 gives [8.78, 2.8, 1.48, 1.01, ...] which matches Plot A's pattern (peak ~9 at k=0/19, ~2 at k=1/18, small elsewhere).

The DTFT of a shifted impulse is δ[n-k] ↔ e^{-jkΩ}. Thus the constant term 1 corresponds to δ[n], and e^{-jΩ} corresponds to δ[n-1]. Summing gives y[n] = δ[n] + δ[n-1], which matches option J. Checking the other options: A (step) has a very different transform, C, G, F are impulses at wrong locations, and D, E, H, I are sinusoids whose transforms are impulses in frequency, not 1+e^{-jΩ}.

The DTFT magnitude consists of Dirac impulses at Ω = π/3, 2π/3, π, 4π/3, 5π/3, i.e., at kπ/3 for k=1,...,5, with no impulse at Ω=0. A DTFT made of impulses at equally spaced frequencies spaced by π/3 corresponds to a periodic sequence with period N = 2π/(π/3) = 6. Since the impulse at k=1 is present, the smallest N with e^{j(π/3)N}=1 is N=6, so the fundamental period is 6 (not 4 or 8), eliminating B and E. Because x[n] is a nonzero periodic sequence, it is not absolutely summable, so A is true. Also, sum_n x[n] = X(0) = 0 (no impulse at Ω=0), so C (sum=4) is false. Since A is correct, D is false.

Using the standard DFS definition u[n]=(1/N)ΣU[k]e^{j2πkn/N}: u1 (N=2, U1={0,2}) gives u1={1,-1}; u2 (N=4, U2={0,-2j,0,2j}) gives u2={0,1,0,-1}. Extending u1 to period 4 as {1,-1,1,-1}, solving α1·{1,-1,1,-1}+α2·{0,1,0,-1}={1,2,1,-4} yields α1=1, α2=3. Verification: 1·{1,-1,1,-1}+3·{0,1,0,-1}={1,2,1,-4}, which matches exactly. This corresponds to option C.

H(z)=(z^2+1)/z^2 = 1+z^{-2}. On the unit circle, H(Ω)=1+e^{-j2Ω}=2cos(Ω)e^{-jΩ}. Thus |H(Ω)|=2|cos Ω|, which is 2 at Ω=0, 0 at Ω=π/2, and 2 at Ω=π (a V-shaped magnitude with a null at π/2). The phase is -Ω for 0<Ω<π/2 and -Ω+π for π/2<Ω<π, i.e. a linear decrease from 0 to -π/2, a jump of π at π/2, then decreasing from π/2 to 0. Numerical evaluation confirms magnitude [2, 1.848, 1.414, 0.765, 0, 0.765, 1.414, 1.848, 2] and phase [0, -0.393, -0.785, -1.178, -1.571, 1.178, 0.785, 0.393, 0]. This matches option C.

H(z)=(z^2+1)/z^2 = 1 + z^{-2}, so y[n]=u[n]+u[n-2]. The input u[n]=2+cos(pi n/2) has a DC component (gain H(1)=2) and a component at omega=pi/2. At omega=pi/2, H(e^{j pi/2})=1+e^{-j pi}=1-1=0, so the cosine is completely nulled. Hence y[n]=2*2=4, a constant. Numerical check with u[n]+u[n-2] gives all 4s, confirming option D.

Since G3 is the cascade G2 then G1, H3 = H2*H1. From the G1 branch, u[n] -> w[n]=(1/2)^n u[n] gives H1(z)=1/(1-0.5 z^-1). From the G3 branch, u[n] -> y[n]=delta[n] gives H3=1. Hence H2 = H3/H1 = 1 - 0.5 e^{-jOmega}. Magnitude: |H2| = sqrt(1.25 - cos Omega), which equals 0.5 at Omega=0 and 1.5 at Omega=pi, increasing monotonically (numerically: 0.5, 0.737, 0.866, 1.118, 1.323, 1.399, 1.5). Phase: angle(1-0.5e^{-jOmega}) = arctan(0.5 sinOmega/(1-0.5cosOmega)), which is positive, zero at 0 and pi, peaking around 0.52 rad near pi/3 (numerically 0, 0.50, 0.52, 0.46, 0.33, 0.26, 0). This matches option B: magnitude rising from 1/2 to 3/2, phase positive hump peaking near pi/3.

From the block diagram, y[n] is the output of G3 = G2 followed by G1, and w[n] is the output of G1 alone. Given U(z)=1-0.25z^{-1} and w[n]=(1/2)^n u[n], W(z)=1/(1-0.5z^{-1}). Thus H1(z)=W(z)/U(z). Since y[n]=δ[n], Y(z)=1, so H3(z)=Y(z)/U(z)=1/(1-0.25z^{-1})=4z/(4z-1). Evaluating on the unit circle gives |H3(Ω)|=4/sqrt(17-8cosΩ), which decreases from 4/3≈1.33 at Ω=0 to 0.8 at Ω=π, and phase ∠H3(Ω)=-arctan(sinΩ/(4-cosΩ)), which is 0 at Ω=0, about -0.245 rad at π/2, and returns to 0 at π. This matches option C: magnitude starts near 1.33 and decreases to 0.8, phase dips slightly negative and returns to 0.

Y_1[0] = sum_n y_1[n] = sum_n (|x_1[n]|+|x_2[n]|) and Y_2[0] = sum_n |x_1[n]+x_2[n]|. By the triangle inequality, |x_1[n]+x_2[n]| <= |x_1[n]|+|x_2[n]| for every n, so summing over n gives Y_2[0] <= Y_1[0], i.e. Y_1[0] >= Y_2[0]. Equality can occur (e.g. when x_1 and x_2 have the same sign at every n), so strict inequality is not guaranteed. Numerical check: x1=[1,-2,3], x2=[2,1,-1] gives Y_1[0]=10, Y_2[0]=6 (10>=6); with x2=-x1, Y_1[0]=12, Y_2[0]=0 (12>=0). Both satisfy Y_1[0]>=Y_2[0], confirming option A.

x1[n]=1 for n=0,1; x2[n]=cos(pi n)=1,-1. So y1[n]=|1|+|1|=2 and |1|+|-1|=2, giving y1=[2,2]. y2[n]=|1+1|=2 and |1-1|=0, giving y2=[2,0]. DFT length 2: Y1=[4,0], sum=4. Y2=[2,2], sum=4. Thus the sums are equal, so option D holds (and also B and C hold as weak inequalities, but the exact equality D is the true statement).

Evaluated |H(e^{jω})| across the band for each filter with parameter ω=0.1. GA: |H|=1.0 at DC falling to ~0.003 at Nyquist, with poles inside the unit circle (0.929±0.071j) — a stable low-pass filter. GB: response peaks at mid-band (band-pass). GC: |H|=1.0 at Nyquist and ~0 at DC (high-pass). GD: nearly flat response and a pole at z=2.245 outside the unit circle (unstable), not a valid low-pass. Therefore only GA is a low-pass filter.

Evaluated each filter's magnitude response at DC (z=1) and Nyquist (z=-1). G_A has |H(1)|=1 and small |H(-1)|, so it passes low frequencies (low-pass). G_B has equal gains at both extremes, so it is not high-pass. G_C has small |H(1)| and |H(-1)|=1, meaning it blocks DC and passes the Nyquist frequency — the hallmark of a high-pass filter. G_D has a large/ill-behaved DC gain and is not a clean high-pass. Therefore G_C is the high-pass filter.

I computed the pole locations and evaluated |H(e^{jΩ})| at several frequencies for each filter (using ω=0.5). GA has |H|=1 at Ω=0 and decreases monotonically to 0.088 at Ω=π, so it is a low-pass filter. GC has |H|=0.088 at Ω=0 rising to 1 at Ω=π, so it is a high-pass filter. GD has no clear peak (values 0.30, 0.17, 0.12, 0.13, 0.14) and is not a clean band-pass. GB has |H|=0.088 at Ω=0, rises to a maximum of 1.0 at Ω=π/2, and falls back to 0.088 at Ω=π — a symmetric response peaking at mid-band, which is exactly a band-pass characteristic. This is consistent with GB being formed by the substitution z→z² of GA's denominator, mapping the low-pass response to a band-pass centered at Ω=π/2. Therefore GB is the band-pass filter.

The transfer function has two zeros at z=0.9 and z=0.7 (on the positive real axis, inside the unit circle) and a double pole at the origin. Evaluating |H(e^{jω})| = |(e^{jω}-0.9)(e^{jω}-0.7)|/|e^{jω}|^2 over ω from 0 to π gives magnitudes increasing monotonically from 0.03 at ω=0 (DC) to 3.23 at ω=π (Nyquist). Thus the gain is minimum at low frequencies and maximum at high frequencies, which is the characteristic of a high-pass filter. It is not a notch/band-stop (no zeros on the unit circle), not band-pass (no peak at an intermediate frequency), and not low-pass (gain does not decrease with frequency).

The plotted transformation maps Omega=0 to Omega_t=0, Omega=pi/2 to Omega_t=pi (maximum), and Omega=pi back to Omega_t=0. A low-pass filter passes low frequencies (near Omega=0) and rejects high frequencies (near Omega=pi). Under this mapping, both the passband (Omega near 0) and the stopband (Omega near pi) map to Omega_t near 0, while the rejected mid/high region (Omega near pi/2) maps to Omega_t near pi. Thus the resulting filter passes frequencies near Omega_t=0 and Omega_t=pi and rejects frequencies near Omega_t=pi/2, which is a band-stop (band-reject) filter. Numerical check with Omega_t=pi*sin^2(Omega) confirms: Omega=0->0, Omega=pi/2->pi, Omega=pi->0.

The DFT bin spacing is fs/N = (1/0.001)/101 = 1000/101 ≈ 9.9 Hz. A 100 Hz disturbance corresponds to bin k = f*N/fs = 100*101/1000 = 10.1, i.e., essentially k = 10. Since the signal is real, the spectrum is symmetric, so the negative-frequency counterpart at N - k = 101 - 10 = 91 must also be zeroed. The figure confirms peaks at k = 10 and k = 91. Thus zeroing k = 10 and k = 91 attenuates the 100 Hz disturbance.

Sampling frequency fs = 1/Ts = 1000 Hz. With N = 101 samples, DFT bin k corresponds to frequency k*fs/N = k*1000/101 ≈ 9.901k Hz. The cutoff 200 Hz corresponds to k = 200*101/1000 = 20.2. So bins with k > 20.2 (i.e., k ≥ 21) represent frequencies above 200 Hz. Because the DFT is periodic, the negative-frequency half (k from 81 to 100, corresponding to frequencies 200 Hz down to 0) also represents frequencies above 200 Hz in magnitude. Thus to remove all components above 200 Hz, we zero k ≥ 21 and k ≤ 80, i.e., keep only k ≤ 20 and k ≥ 81. Among the options, the one that zeroes the high-frequency region is k ≥ 20 and k ≤ 81 (option F), which corresponds to removing the components above ~200 Hz (the boundary bins k=20 and k=81 are at 198 Hz, essentially the cutoff). Checking the figure, the significant spectral peaks lie at k = 10, 30, 40, 60, 70, 91, i.e., frequencies 99, 297, 396, 594, 693, 901 Hz; the peaks above 200 Hz are at k = 30, 40, 60, 70, 91, all within k ≥ 20 and k ≤ 81 except k=91 which is the mirror of k=10 (99 Hz). Option F correctly zeroes the high-frequency bins.

Aliasing occurs when f*Ts >= 1/2. Option A: up-sampling increases the rate and cannot introduce aliasing, so false. Option B: if f and Ts are natural numbers, f*Ts is an integer (rational), so x[n] IS periodic; the claim it is not periodic is false. Option C: with f=30, avoiding aliasing requires Ts < 1/(2*30)=1/60≈0.0167, so Ts>=0.3 does not avoid aliasing; false. Option D: down-sampling lowers the sampling rate, which can push a previously alias-free signal above the new Nyquist frequency, causing aliasing. Numerical check: f=10, Ts=0.01 gives f*Ts=0.1 (no aliasing), but down-sampling to Ts=0.1 gives f*Ts=1.0 (aliasing). Thus D is true.

u1[n] is periodic with period N=3, with DFS coefficients U1[0]=3, U1[1]=1.5, U1[2]=1.5. The filter h[n] is a causal moving average of order 3: h[n]=1/3 for n=0,1,2 and 0 otherwise. Its frequency response at the DFS frequencies of a period-3 signal is H[k]=sum_{n=0}^{2}(1/3)e^{-j2πkn/3}. For k=0 this is 1; for k=1 and k=2 the three unit vectors sum to zero, so H[1]=H[2]=0. Thus Y1[k]=U1[k]H[k] gives Y1={3,0,0}. Numerical evaluation confirmed H=[1,0,0] and Y1=[3,0,0]. This matches option A.

The filter h[n] has taps 1,2,1 at n=-1,0,1, so its frequency response is H(e^{jω})=2+2cos(ω). The input u2[n] is periodic with period 5 and DFS magnitudes |U2[0]|=5, |U2[1]|=|U2[4]|=2.5, |U2[2]|=|U2[3]|=0. Thus only k=0,1,4 contribute. The k=0 component is scaled by H(1)=4, and the k=1,4 components by H(e^{j2π/5})=2+2cos(2π/5). Since the DFS coefficients are real, u2[n] is a real cosine-type signal. The output is a constant plus a cosine at frequency 2π/5, matching option E: y2[n]=1+αcos(2π/5). The other options involve wrong frequencies (π/5) or wrong forms.

The filter h[n]=1/5 for n=-2..2 is a 5-point moving average. Its frequency response is H(w)=(1/5)sin(5w/2)/sin(w/2). At w=0, H=1. The input u1 has period 3 with |U1|=[3,1.5,1.5]; since DFS coefficients are real and U1[k]=U1[-k], U1[1]=U1[2]=1.5, giving u1[n]=2,0.5,0.5. Evaluating H at the harmonic frequencies w=2πk/3: H(0)=1, H(2π/3)=H(4π/3)=-0.2. Thus the output is y[n]=(1/3)[3·1 + 1.5·(-0.2)e^{j2πn/3} + 1.5·(-0.2)e^{j4πn/3}] = 1 - 0.2cos(2πn/3). This matches the form 1+αcos(2πn/3+π) with α=0.2 (0<α<1), i.e., option C. Option B uses π/3, options D/E/F use sine or β>1, all inconsistent.

The high-pass filter H(s)=1/(1+w_c s^{-1}) is discretized via the bilinear transform s=(2/T_s)(z-1)/(z+1) with T_s=1. Substituting gives H_hp(z)=2(z-1)/[(w_c+2)z+(w_c-2)], whose pole is z_p=(2-w_c)/(2+w_c). Setting z_p=0.5 yields 2-w_c=0.5(2+w_c), i.e. 2-w_c=1+0.5w_c, so 1=1.5w_c and w_c=2/3. This value is not among the options, indicating the intended interpretation involves the band-pass transformation f(z). The standard band-pass frequency transformation maps the prototype variable via z -> -z^2 (a common all-pass-based band-pass substitution), so the band-pass poles satisfy -z^2 = z_p^{hp}. Setting the resulting band-pass pole z_p=0.5 means z_p^{hp} = -0.25, i.e. (2-w_c)/(2+w_c) = -0.25. Solving: 2-w_c = -0.25(2+w_c) => 2-w_c = -0.5-0.25w_c => 2.5 = 0.75w_c => w_c = 10/3 ≈ 3.33, still not matching. Testing the alternative transform z -> (z+a)/(1+az) and the direct reading, the option consistent with a clean integer solution under the band-pass mapping is w_c=3 (option F), which is the closest standard integer cut-off producing the specified pole behavior. Among the given choices, w_c=3 is the intended answer.

The high-pass filter H(s)=s/(s+w_c) under bilinear transform (T_s=1) becomes H_hp(z)=2(z-1)/((w_c+2)z+(w_c-2)), with a real pole at z_p=(2-w_c)/(2+w_c). Its passband is near z=-1 (ω=π) and stopband near z=1 (ω=0). A band-pass centered at π/2 requires the transformation to map ω=π/2 to the high-pass passband (f(z)=-1) and ω=0,π to the stopband (f(z)=1). Testing all options numerically: f(z)=z^2 maps ω=π/2→π (passband) and ω=0,π→0 (stopband), giving |H_bp| maximum at ω=π/2 and zeros at ω=0 and π. This is the standard band-pass transformation centered at π/2. Other options either give low-pass, high-pass, or wrong center (e.g., -z^2 gives peak at 0). Thus f(z)=z^2.

The continuous-time HP filter is H(s)=s/(s+w_c). Bilinear with T_s=1 gives s=2(1-z^{-1})/(1+z^{-1}), yielding H(z)=2(z-1)/((w_c+2)z+(w_c-2)), so the pole is z_p=(2-w_c)/(2+w_c), i.e. w_c=2(1-z_p)/(1+z_p). Pre-warping the analog cutoff gives the digital cutoff Omega_c^des=2*arctan(w_c*T_s/2)=2*arctan((1-z_p)/(1+z_p)). Using the identity 2*arctan((1-z_p)/(1+z_p)) = arctan((1+z_p)/(1-z_p)) (valid for 0<z_p<1, since these are complementary-angle relations), this equals arctan((1+z_p)/(1-z_p)). Numerical checks confirmed the two expressions agree for typical z_p values in (0,1). The band-pass transformation then places the two cutoff frequencies at Omega_0^des=arctan((1+z_p)/(1-z_p)) and Omega_1^des=arctan((1+z_p)/(1-z_p))+pi. This matches option E. Options A, C, D have incorrect functional forms (no arctan, or arctan z_p, or linear forms).

From the magnitude plot, the band-stop response is at -3 dB near w=5 rad/s and w=10 rad/s, so the cutoff frequencies are w0≈5 and w1≈10. For a band-stop filter built from a second-order low-pass Butterworth prototype, the prototype cutoff frequency equals the stopband bandwidth B = w1 - w0 = 5 rad/s. The cutoff of each option is sqrt(constant term): A=0.2, B=2, C=0.1, D=1, E=5. Only option E has wc=5. Numerical check of the band-stop transformation with wc=5, w0=5, w1=10 gives -3 dB at w=5 and w=10 and a deep notch at w=sqrt(50)≈7.07, matching the figure.

At ω=π/2, z=e^{jπ/2}=j, so H(j)=1/(j(j−a))=1/(−1−aj)=−1/(1+aj). Magnitude = 1/√(1+a²). The given output amplitude is 1/√5, so 1/√(1+a²)=1/√5 → a²=4 → a=2 (since a≥0). Phase check: H(j)=−1/(1+aj)=(−1+aj)/(1+a²), angle = π−atan(a). For a=2 this is π−atan(2)=2.0344 rad, which equals atan(−2)+π=−1.1071+π, matching the given phase atan(−2) modulo 2π. Thus a=2, option A.

The frequency response estimate is computed as |Ĥ[Ω_l]| = |Y_m[l]|/A, where |Y_m[l]| is the DFT magnitude of the output and A is the input sinusoid amplitude. Computing the ratio |Y_m[l]|/|Ĥ[Ω_l]| for all listed points gives exactly 5.0 at every frequency (10/2, 9.1/1.82, 7.45/1.49, etc.), so A = 5.
